archetype.name: Title Contender (Wembanyama-anchored, defense-first)
archetype.definition: A team coming off a 62-20 season and a deep playoff run, built around the league's top-ranked center, whose defense and ball security give it a high floor while the offense finds its level.

report.headline: Defense travels, offense lags last year: still a contender after a wobbly start
report.take:
San Antonio arrives as the measuring stick. Last season was 62-20, first on the site and 13 playoff wins, and six games into this one the Spurs are 4-2 with the league's 8th-best Net Rtg at 7.1. The start was clumsy: home losses to OKC and HOU. Then came four straight wins by comfortable margins, except the overtime game in Utah. The record is no fluke in either direction. W vs Pt Diff is 0, and the margin implies exactly the 4 wins they have.

The engine has shifted from last year. That team ranked 4th on offense and 3rd on defense. This one is 7th on defense with a 108.7 DRtg, well below the league's 113.1, and a more modest 115.8 ORtg. The defense works the way a Wembanyama defense should. Opponents get to the rim less than average and shoot 61.6% there, and the Spurs clean up the glass with a 75.8 DRB %, 7th in the league. Opposing centers and power forwards are pulling down well under their usual rebounds. On offense the hidden weapon is ball security, a 11.7 TOV % that ranks 2nd. That covers for a shot profile that is light on threes and free throws.

The numbers hide how concentrated this is. Wembanyama is 1st on the center tab with a 9.5 BPM and a +36.2 On-Off, and Fox's +30.9 On-Off and 68.6 TS % make him the other pillar. Yet the frontcourt grades D+. Everything behind Wembanyama is underwater: Kornet's On-Off is -41.8, and Bryant and Barnes are deep in the red too. Those non-Wembanyama minutes are where the Spurs lose games. On the other side, opponents are hitting 37.3% from three, 23rd in the league and well above last year's 35.2. That looks more like early variance than a structural leak, and it should drift back toward the team's favor.

Where is this heading? The season pace says 55 wins. That is a sensible floor for a team whose underlying defense is real and whose offense sits far below last season's 119.6 ORtg with largely the same core. The last five games show the correction already under way, at plus 11 a game. If the shooting luck on defense evens out and the offense creeps back toward last year's level, this is a top-five team by Net Rtg again.

strengths.title: Wembanyama-built interior defense
strengths.body: Opponents take fewer shots at the rim than average and convert them poorly. The DRB % ranks 7th, so second chances are scarce. Opposing bigs are rebounding well below their norms. This is the same profile as last year's 3rd-ranked defense (62.2 Opp Rim FG % then), so it is structural, not a six-game blip.

strengths.title: Elite ball security
strengths.body: An 11.7 TOV % ranks 2nd, well under the league's 14. With Fox (42 assists) and Harper running things, the Spurs rarely give away possessions. That keeps a middling shooting offense at 9th in ORtg. The Spurs were similarly careful last year at 11.8, so expect it to hold.

strengths.title: Two stars plus a hot wing
strengths.body: Wembanyama carries a 34.5 USG % with a 9.5 BPM, and Fox scores efficiently at a 68.6 TS %. Champagnie is 3rd on the wing tab, shooting 71.8 TS % with 20 threes. That shooting is the part most likely to cool. The two stars' On-Off numbers, both above +30, show where the team's identity lives.

concerns.title: Collapse when Wembanyama sits
concerns.body: The frontcourt grade is D+ despite the top-ranked center on the tab. Kornet's -41.8 On-Off and the negative marks for Bryant and Barnes show the backup bigs giving games away. Six games exaggerate On-Off swings. Still, every frontcourt reserve ranks near the bottom of his tab, so this is the roster's real soft spot.

concerns.title: Offense well off last year
concerns.body: ORtg is 115.8 against last season's 119.6, and TS % has slipped to 56.8 from 59.5. The shot diet is thin on threes (3PA Rate 24th) and free throws (FT Rate 23rd). Castle's 50.9 TS % with a team-high guard usage is part of it. The core is unchanged, so some of this should come back, but the low free-throw rate has been a Spurs trait for years.

concerns.title: Opponents hitting from deep
concerns.body: Opponents are shooting 37.3% from three, 23rd in the league and above the league's 34.9. The defense otherwise grades well, so this reads mostly as variance that should regress in San Antonio's favor. It is worth watching against high-volume shooting teams.

trend.note: Two home losses to open, then four straight wins. The last five games run at plus 11 a game, well above the season mark, as the defense settled in.

weekAhead.headline: Four soft spots and Portland: a week to bank wins
weekAhead.body:
Five games: Utah and Dallas at home, then a road swing through Sacramento, Portland and Phoenix. Three of the five opponents sit 26th or worse on the site. The Spurs already beat Utah, Dallas and Sacramento in October, and won the last two of those comfortably. Sacramento (0-6, 124.0 DRtg) and Phoenix (126.3 DRtg, last in the league) are the kind of defenses that let a stagnant offense rediscover its rhythm.

The real test is Portland on the second night of a back-to-back after Sacramento. The Blazers are 2nd on the site with an 11.4 Net Rtg, lead the league in 3PA Rate, get to the line at the 3rd-best rate and grade A in the frontcourt. That is exactly the profile that probes San Antonio's three-point defense and its thin bench bigs. Dallas is no pushover either: a 56.9 eFG % and a 29.7 Opp 3P % make it a tougher home game than its site rank suggests. Anything less than four wins would be a disappointment.

keyMatchups.title: Portland's volume threes on a back-to-back
keyMatchups.body: Portland takes more threes than anyone and defends point guards brutally, holding them well under their usual production. That squeezes Fox and Castle. The opening is inside: the Blazers allow 24.0 points a game to centers, among the most in the league, so Wembanyama should be the focal point.

keyMatchups.title: Phoenix leaking to guards and bigs
keyMatchups.body: Phoenix owns the league's worst DRtg and gives up 46.5 points a game to point guards, last in the league. Centers also feast on the boards against them. Fox and Wembanyama should both have big nights, though the Suns' 57.4 Opp Rim FG % ranks 1st, so Wembanyama may need to score away from the basket.

keyMatchups.title: Utah walls off centers
keyMatchups.body: Utah is 1-5 but holds centers far below their usual production and has allowed the league's lowest Opp Rim Rate. The Jazz leak to shooting guards instead, at 37.5 points a game. That is Harper's and Vassell's night to carry the scoring if Utah packs the paint against Wembanyama again.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the non-Wembanyama minutes hold up on the Sacramento–Portland back-to-back, where bench big men will have to play real time.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense, the low turnover rate and the two-star core are real and repeatable, carried over from a 62-20 season. The offense, well below last year's level, is the part most likely to improve, and opponents' hot three-point shooting should cool. Against that, Champagnie's shooting will come down, and the bench frontcourt is a genuine weakness that only gets exposed further over 76 more games.

A reasonable expectation is a top-eight Net Rtg team that finishes in the mid-to-high 50s in wins. The Southwest is crowded early, with Memphis and Houston unbeaten or close to it, so the division is not a given. Health and minutes for Wembanyama dominate everything else: the team's margin with him on the floor is what makes it a contender.
swingFactors: Whether the offense recovers toward last year's efficiency

confidence.note: Only six games, but last season's profile strongly backs the defense.
